newsitem.title: FRANCE: Brittan asks Danes to back EU on US anti-Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: Brittan asks Danes to back EU on US anti-Cuba law.

text.p: European Union Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan urged Denmark on Thursday to fall back into line with the other 14 European Union member states in their joint stand against U.S. anti-Cuba trade laws.
"I hope our Danish colleagues will help us reach a position by unanimity, which is needed to react," Brittan said at a European forum lunch in Paris.
"I understand the Danish problem but I have to say I hope Denmark will reconsider its position in the coming days."

Denmark shattered a common European Union stand on Tuesday when it said it would veto proposals for retaliation against the U.S. policy just days before they were due to be set in stone by EU foreign ministers.

Brittan has spearheaded the European campaign against the U.S. crackdown on Havana on the grounds that Washington has no right to punish foreign firms from other parts of the globe which do business in Cuba.

Like Canada, Mexico and others, the EU vehemently opposes the U.S. Helm-Burton law, which would tighten the screws further on Havana by opening the way for Americans to take legal action against any foreign firms making money from property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.

President Bill Clinton has put the bulk of the legislation on hold until the end of the year while cranking the U.S. diplomatic machine into action to sell the policy as a campaign for democracy and human rights in Cuba.
Brittan told his Paris audience he had been in touch with Danish ministers, that the veto was not one of principle and he hoped Copenhagen would find a way round the problem.
"They (Denmark) agree on the principle," Brittan said.

Copenhagen says it cannot go along with EU action based on a catch-all clause in the EU's founding treaties, which is regarded with suspicion by governments wary of ceding too much authority to the EU bloc.
The latest hiccup in the EU's attempts to act as a single cohesive group has highlighted the debate about whether more issues should be voted by majority rather than unanimity in the 15-nation bloc.
After similar calls from European Commission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday, Brittan said he saw a need for more decision-taking by qualified majority in the EU.
